name: Pan-Africanism
summary: Pan-Africanism holds that Africans and people of African descent form one people with a common cause: ending colonial rule, racism and neo-colonial control, winning self-government for African peoples, and uniting the continent politically. The Pan-African Congresses (1900-1945), Nkrumah's call for a union government, the OAU and the African Union state this cause; its economics and domestic politics vary by strand, and its documents say little on social and moral questions.
scope: The doctrine on the African national question: self-determination, colonialism and neo-colonialism, sovereignty and borders, continental union, race and equality, the diaspora, culture, and the means of liberation. Based on the Pan-African Congress documents (Du Bois, 1919-1927; Manchester 1945), Nkrumah's writings and speeches, Garvey's Philosophy and Opinions, the OAU Charter, the Constitutive Act and Agenda 2063. Full programmes of Nkrumah's Ghana, the AU or any party (economy, welfare, social policy) are not taken as the doctrine; economic answers rest only on demands the Congress resolutions themselves state, and Nkrumah's socialism and one-party state are left unanswered as one strand's programme. Garveyite emigrationism is used only where it is shown to differ or agree.

bound-labor.rationale: Manchester 1945 demanded the abolition of forced labour in East Africa and condemned systems that bind Africans to labour for alien rulers.

civilizational-union.rationale: Agenda 2063 grounds political unity in a common history, destiny, identity and heritage of African peoples; the unity claimed is continental and rests on shared culture, not on one religion.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Manchester 1945 said the claims of partnership, trusteeship, guardianship and the mandate system do not serve Africans, and demanded independence; Nkrumah called the civilising mission a cloak for robbery. Du Bois's 1919 memorandum had still allowed gradual autonomy under League oversight, so the early Congresses were softer.

collective-defense.rationale: The Constitutive Act commits the Union to a common defence policy for the continent, and the 1961 Ghana-Guinea-Mali charter provides joint defence in favour of any member that is attacked; the Charter itself speaks of cooperation for defence and security.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: Du Bois's 1927 resolutions demand the development of Africa for the Africans and not merely for the profit of Europeans, and Manchester 1945 condemned systematic imperial exploitation of colonies.

common-currency.rationale: Nkrumah's OAU speech proposes an African currency, monetary zone and central bank, and Article 19 of the Constitutive Act creates an African Central Bank and Monetary Fund.

consent-of-governed.rationale: The 1945 Declaration to Colonial Workers says colonial peoples must have the right to elect their own governments without restriction by foreign powers, and rejects rule imposed by an outside power.

democracy-best.rationale: The Constitutive Act pledges respect for democratic principles and condemns unconstitutional changes of government, and Agenda 2063 calls for a universal culture of democratic values; the texts do not discuss a majority choosing badly.

diaspora-return-right.rationale: Garvey looked to the day American and West Indian Negroes settle in Africa, and a Jamaican UNIA resolution before the 1945 Congress asked the removal of barriers to people of African descent entering and domiciling in Africa.

dominated-front.rationale: Padmore's report on the 1945 Congress looks to a Colonial and Coloured Peoples' Freedom Front joining African and Asian liberation movements, and the Congress pledged solidarity with Indonesia, Vietnam and India.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: The 1921 manifesto asks the League to take a firm stand on the absolute equality of races, and Manchester 1945 demanded full equality of rights for all citizens regardless of race, culture and sex.

farm-price-support.rationale: The West Indian resolutions demanded guaranteed fair minimum prices and marketing facilities for farm produce, and a banking system giving cheap long-term credit to agriculture.

history-own-civilization.rationale: Nkrumah's Africa Must Unite says Ghana must replace colonial textbooks and nurture its own culture and history to build the African personality that should be the educational foundation of a Pan-African future.

independence-needs-economic-change.rationale: Nkrumah's OAU speech says independence is only the prelude to a struggle to run our own economic and social affairs free of neo-colonial controls, and the Congress demanded freedom from foreign control 'political or economic'. This does not call for changing the property system itself.

independent-unions.rationale: Manchester 1945 complained that West African workers were denied trade unions free of official interference and urged colonial unions to organise; Nkrumah's Ghana tied unions closely to the ruling party.

indigenous-land-authority.rationale: Du Bois's 1927 and 1919 texts demand native rights to the land and natural resources, and Manchester 1945 resolved that West African land is the rightful property of its people.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: A Gold Coast society's message to the 1945 Congress held that self-government need not follow English models; the Congress itself did not adopt a general view.

job-guarantee.rationale: The West Indian resolutions demanded state departments to develop natural resources so as to give regular employment at living wages to all men and women able and willing to work.

keep-colonial-borders.rationale: The OAU Charter and the Constitutive Act (Article 4(b)) respect borders existing at independence, while the Manchester Congress called the colonial boundaries artificial divisions meant to obstruct West African unity: the sources point both ways.

local-essentials-public.rationale: The West Indian resolutions demanded public ownership of public utilities, such as transportation, and organised water supplies in rural areas.

national-resource-control.rationale: Du Bois's 1927 resolutions demand native rights to the land and natural resources, Manchester 1945 protested that mines are in foreign monopoly hands, and the OAU Charter commits states to harness Africa's own resources.

national-self-determination.rationale: The Fifth Congress declared the right of all peoples to govern themselves and demanded complete independence for every colony; the OAU Charter opens on the inalienable right of all peoples to control their destiny.

no-foreign-bases.rationale: In his OAU speech Nkrumah says the search for bases and spheres of influence brings the Cold War into Africa and that neo-colonialists use their bases to entrench themselves; Africa Must Unite treats foreign bases on African soil as a mark of nominal independence.

no-nuclear-weapons-on-territory.rationale: Nkrumah told the 1963 founding summit that Africa should be declared a nuclear-free zone and freed from Cold War exigencies.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Africa Must Unite calls it paradoxical that African states cling to sovereignty while Europe makes concessions to supranational bodies, and the OAU speech and Constitutive Act call for a continental union with common institutions and a central bank.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: The Union of African States charter in Africa Must Unite makes rehabilitation and development of African culture a task of the union, and Agenda 2063 aims at restoring and preserving Africa's cultural heritage, including its languages.

production-for-use.rationale: Manchester 1945 condemned the rule of private wealth and industry for private profit alone, and Du Bois's 1927 resolutions call for commerce and industry to serve the welfare of the many rather than the enriching of the few.

property-franchise.rationale: The West Indian resolutions adopted at Manchester demanded universal adult suffrage and the removal of all property and income qualifications for public office.

public-ownership.rationale: The West Indian resolutions adopted at Manchester demanded nationalisation of all basic industries and public ownership of public utilities such as transport.

racial-franchise.rationale: Manchester 1945 demanded that every man and woman over 21 in Kenya and South Africa elect and be elected to the legislature with no distinction of race.

racial-group-interests.rationale: Du Bois's 1927 resolutions urge Black voters in the US to vote for the international problems of the colour line and to organise politically; Garvey urged each race to act for itself.

racial-pride.rationale: Garvey's writings centre on pride in the Negro race and its redemption, and Du Bois's 1915 words quoted at the 1945 Congress speak of a strong brotherhood of Negro blood.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: The 1945 Congress condemned South Africa's racial laws, with one system of law for 'Aryans' and another for non-whites, as essentially fascist, and demanded the franchise and full equality for non-Europeans.

restrict-indigenous-settlement.rationale: Manchester 1945 demanded the immediate cessation of further European settlement in Kenya and the rest of East Africa and the return of land to landless Africans.

restructure-world-economy.rationale: Agenda 2063 aims at improving Africa's place in the global governance system, including the financial institutions, and the Constitutive Act seeks conditions for Africa to play its rightful role in the global economy and international negotiations.

right-to-secede.rationale: Nkrumah condemns balkanisation and the secession of Katanga as neo-colonial devices, and the OAU Charter and Constitutive Act pledge defence of member states' territorial integrity.

rights-where-you-live.rationale: The 1945 Congress backed Afro-Americans' fight for full citizenship in the US, while Garvey's movement looked to settlement in Africa; the strands diverge on this.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: Article III(7) of the OAU Charter affirms a policy of non-alignment with regard to all blocs, and Nkrumah's 1963 OAU speech calls non-alignment an article of faith on the continent.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: The West Indian resolutions at Manchester demanded an increase in the rate of taxes on higher income groups.

unions-good.rationale: The 1945 Declaration to Colonial Workers urges workers to organise, calls trade union rights a means by which liberties are won, and names the strike and boycott invincible weapons.

universal-healthcare.rationale: The East African resolutions demanded a state medical, health and welfare service available to all, and the West Indian ones demanded national health insurance.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: The 1945 Congress endorsed opposition to unequal distribution of wealth and the rule of wealth, and welcomed economic democracy as the only real democracy.

women-suffrage.rationale: Manchester 1945 demanded the franchise for every man and woman over 21 in East Africa and South Africa and universal adult suffrage in the West Indies.

world-economy-extracts-surplus.rationale: Manchester 1945 resolved that imperial powers systematically exploited Africa's resources to the detriment of the inhabitants, and Nkrumah's Neo-Colonialism argues that foreign capital and trade keep Africa poor while enriching others.

missingStatements.text: The states of a continent should merge into a single continental government.
missingStatements.rationale: Nkrumah's OAU speech calls for a union government of African states with common defence, foreign policy, currency and planning; the Constitutive Act pledges accelerated political integration.

missingStatements.text: A continent should be declared a nuclear-weapon-free zone.
missingStatements.rationale: Nkrumah told the 1963 OAU summit that Africa should be declared a nuclear-free zone.

notes: Searched all themes in the Congress documents, Nkrumah's books and speeches, Garvey, the OAU Charter, Constitutive Act and Agenda 2063; positions exist chiefly on self-determination, colonialism, borders and union, race and rights, the diaspora, culture, means, and the economic demands of the 1945 resolutions. Strands differ on borders (Manchester against the OAU/AU respect for colonial borders), on staying or emigrating (Du Bois's NAACP line against Garvey) and on means (Du Bois's 1921 Congress contemplated no force; the 1945 Congress and Nkrumah accepted armed struggle). Nkrumah's one-party state and socialism, Garvey's views on racial purity and the AU's gender-equality and market programme were not counted as the doctrine; they stay null. Several economic and social answers rest on regional resolutions (West Indies, East Africa) that the Fifth Congress adopted and so carry medium confidence at most. The 1919 Du Bois memorandum's tutelage language shows early Congresses softer than later ones.
